title: View Through a Window May Influence Recovery from Surgery
research_question: To determine whether assignment to a room with a window view of a natural setting might have restorative influences on surgical patients' recovery.

participants.description: 46 surgical patients (23 matched pairs, 15 female and 8 male pairs) who underwent cholecystectomy in a suburban Pennsylvania hospital. Patients were aged 20-69 years, had no serious complications, and no history of psychological disturbances.
participants.recruitment: Records of patients between 1972 and 1981 were examined. Patients were selected based on specific criteria (cholecystectomy, May-October surgery, age, no serious complications, no history of psychological disturbances) and then matched by sex, age, smoking status, weight, previous hospitalization, year of surgery, and floor level.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Hospital rooms with windows. One group had a view of a small stand of deciduous trees (natural scene), while the other group had a view of a brown brick wall (built scene). Rooms were otherwise nearly identical in dimensions, window size, arrangement of beds, furniture, and other major physical characteristics.

measures.instrument: Number of days from surgery to discharge
Count of negative evaluative comments in nurses' notes
Number and strength (strong, moderate, weak) of analgesic doses per day
Number and strength of antianxiety drug doses per day
Weighted score of minor complications (e.g., nausea, antacids, inability to move bowels, fever, infection)

findings.antecedent: Window view of a natural scene (trees)
findings.quote: patients with window views of the trees spent less time in the hospital than those with views of the brick wall: 7.96 days compared with 8.70 days per patient

findings.antecedent: Window view of a natural scene (trees)
findings.consequent: Negative evaluative comments in nurses' notes
findings.quote: More negative notes were made on patients with the brick wall view: 3.96 per patient compared to 1.13 per patient with the tree view

findings.antecedent: Window view of a natural scene (trees)
findings.consequent: Positive evaluative comments in nurses' notes
findings.quote: Although more positive comments were recorded for the tree-view patients, the difference was not statistically significant.

findings.consequent: Analgesic intake (strong, moderate, weak doses) on Days 0-1 post-surgery
findings.mechanism: patients would have been too drugged or too absorbed by intense pain to attend to the windows
findings.quote: for the first period no differences in analgesic intake would be found between the two groups

findings.antecedent: Window view of a natural scene (trees)
findings.consequent: Analgesic intake (mean number of doses) on Days 2-5 post-surgery
findings.quote: statistically significant variation between the tree-view and wall-view patients in the mean number of analgesic doses

findings.antecedent: Window view of a natural scene (trees)
findings.consequent: Moderate and strong pain doses on Days 2-5 post-surgery
findings.quote: patients with the tree view took fewer moderate and strong pain doses than did the wall-view group

findings.antecedent: Window view of a natural scene (trees)
findings.consequent: Weak pain doses on Days 2-5 post-surgery
findings.quote: and more doses in the weak category.

findings.consequent: Analgesic intake (strong, moderate, weak doses) on Days 6-7 post-surgery
findings.quote: In the other two periods there were no significant differences.
With respect to doses of antianxiety drugs, there was no significant variation between the groups.

findings.antecedent: Taking two or more strong or moderate analgesic doses on the same day
findings.mechanism: The intake of narcotic analgesics by patients with the wall view may have lowered their use of antianxiety drugs to that of patients with the tree view.
findings.quote: The observed frequency of doses was lower than the expected frequency when two or more strong or moderate analgesics were taken on the same day

findings.antecedent: Window view of a natural scene (trees)
findings.quote: Although tree-view patients had lower scores, the difference was not statistically significant.

mechanisms: Natural views elicit positive feelings, reduce fear, hold interest, and may block or reduce stressful thoughts, fostering restoration from anxiety or stress.
Patients too drugged or absorbed by intense pain may not attend to window views, negating their effect.
Higher intake of narcotic analgesics may reduce the need for antianxiety drugs.
implementation_implications: Hospital design and siting decisions should take into account the quality of patient window views.

tables.description: Comparison of average analgesic doses per patient for wall-view and tree-view groups across three time periods (Days 0-1, Days 2-5, Days 6-7) and three strength levels (Strong, Moderate, Weak).
key_stats: Days 0-1: Strong (Wall 2.56, Tree 2.40), Moderate (Wall 4.00, Tree 5.00), Weak (Wall 0.23, Tree 0.30)
Days 2-5: Strong (Wall 2.48, Tree 0.96), Moderate (Wall 3.65, Tree 1.74), Weak (Wall 2.57, Tree 5.39)
Days 6-7: Strong (Wall 0.22, Tree 0.17), Moderate (Wall 0.35, Tree 0.17), Weak (Wall 0.96, Tree 1.09)

limitations: The 'built' view in this study was a comparatively monotonous, largely featureless brick wall, so conclusions cannot be extended to all built views.
Conclusions may not apply to other patient groups, such as long-term patients, who may suffer from low arousal or boredom rather than anxiety.
Surgery was performed at different times of day and discharge times were somewhat different, potentially affecting length of stay measurement.
Physician matching was only possible for 7 out of 23 pairs due to the large number of doctors.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Records on recovery after cholecystectomy of patients in a suburban Pennsylvania hospital between 1972 and 1981 were examined to determine whether assignment to a room with a window view of a natural setting might have restorative influences. Twenty-three surgical patients assigned to rooms with windows looking out on a natural scene had shorter postoperative hospital stays, received fewer negative evaluative comments in nurses' notes, and took fewer potent analgesics than 23 matched patients in similar rooms with windows facing a brick building wall.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Exposure to natural environments can reduce stress and promote psychological restoration, leading to improved health outcomes.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper implicitly suggests that views of nature reduce psychological stress and provide positive distraction, which in turn facilitates physiological recovery.

steps.to_construct: Improved physiological recovery (e.g., less pain, shorter hospital stay)
